items.prompt: In project management, what does the term "scope" describe?

options.label: The work and deliverables the project includes and excludes
The total amount of money approved for the whole project
The calendar dates on which the project starts and finishes
The group of people who are assigned to the project team

rubric: Scope defines what the project will and will not deliver.
Money, dates and people are other planning elements (budget, schedule, resources), not scope.

items.prompt: Which three elements make up the classic project "triple constraint"?

options.label: Risk, quality and people
Budget, sponsor and team
Plan, execute and close
Scope, time and cost

rubric: The triple constraint is scope, time and cost, which are balanced against each other.
Other options mix in phases, roles or other factors that are not the standard trio.

items.prompt: What is a milestone in a project schedule?

options.label: A limit on spending that applies to one phase only
A task that takes more time than any other task
A regular meeting where the team reports its status
A key point marking progress that has no duration

rubric: A milestone marks a significant point or event and has zero duration.
Learners confuse it with long tasks, status meetings or budget limits.

items.prompt: Which of these best defines a project stakeholder?

options.label: A person or group that provides funding for the project
A person or group that does the work on the project team
Anyone affected by the project or able to influence it
A person or group that formally accepts the final delivery

rubric: Stakeholders include anyone affected by or able to influence the project.
Distractors wrongly narrow the term to funders, team members or the customer alone.

items.prompt: Which planning tool shows tasks as horizontal bars laid out along a timeline?

options.label: Risk matrix
Organisation chart
Pareto chart
Gantt chart

rubric: A Gantt chart displays task durations and sequence as bars against time.
The other tools show defect causes, reporting lines or risk ratings.

items.prompt: Which of the following are recognised phases of the project life cycle? Select all that apply.

options.label: Marketing
Initiating
Closing
Planning
Auditing

rubric: Initiating, planning and closing are standard life cycle phases.
Auditing and marketing are activities, not life cycle phases.

items.prompt: Your manager asks for a document that lists what the project will deliver, what it will not deliver, and the assumptions behind it, so everyone can agree before work starts. Which document is this?

options.label: Lessons-learned log
Scope statement
Status report
Risk register

rubric: The scope statement records deliverables, exclusions and assumptions.
A risk register lists risks, a status report shows progress, and lessons learned come at the end.

items.prompt: Why do project managers create a work breakdown structure (WBS)?

options.label: To break the scope into smaller parts that can be estimated and assigned
To list every identified risk in order of how likely each one is to occur
To record the approvals that senior managers give at each project gate
To rank the team members by how much work each has completed so far

rubric: A WBS decomposes scope into manageable work packages for estimating and assigning.
Distractors describe performance ranking, a risk register or gate approvals.

items.prompt: Which situation is an example of scope creep?

options.label: A team member leaves and another person takes over the role
Extra features are added mid-project without any change review
The team finishes a task earlier than the schedule had planned
The sponsor cuts the budget soon after the project has kicked off

rubric: Scope creep is uncontrolled growth of scope without formal change control.
The other cases are schedule, funding or staffing changes, not scope growth.

items.prompt: A task on the critical path slips by 3 days and nothing else changes. What happens to the project end date?

options.label: It moves later by 1 day
It moves later by 6 days
It moves later by 3 days
It does not change at all

rubric: Critical path tasks have no float, so any slip delays the finish by the same amount.
Distractors assume float or budget changes that the critical path does not have.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a risk from an issue?

options.label: A risk is always a negative event; an issue can be good or bad
A risk is handled by the sponsor; an issue is handled by the team
A risk is a problem that has finished; an issue is one still possible
A risk might happen in the future; an issue is already happening

rubric: A risk is an uncertain future event; an issue has already occurred.
Other options reverse the definitions or invent rules about ownership.

items.prompt: A team adds two extra weeks of testing because they are using an unfamiliar tool and fear defects. Which risk response is this?

options.label: Mitigate
Transfer
Accept
Avoid

rubric: Adding testing time reduces the impact or likelihood of the risk, which is mitigation.
Transfer shifts the risk to a third party, avoid removes the cause, and accept takes no action.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to create a stakeholder communication plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: It removes the need to track risks during the project
It helps bring concerns to light early, before they grow into conflicts
It replaces the project schedule as the main plan
It guarantees that every stakeholder's requests will be met
It sets who needs which information and how often

rubric: A communication plan clarifies information needs and surfaces concerns early.
It does not replace risk tracking, guarantee requests, or substitute for the schedule.

items.prompt: A project has a fixed deadline and a fixed budget. Midway, the client asks for two extra reports. The project manager says the request must go through change control first. Why is this the right step?

options.label: To check the effect on time, cost and scope before agreeing
To confirm the client can pay for the extra reports before any work starts
To record the request so the team can add it quietly to the next release
To get the sponsor to reject small requests so the plan never changes

rubric: Change control assesses the impact on the triple constraint before approval.
Distractors treat it as a penalty, a show of power or a blanket delay, which it is not.

items.prompt: Midway through a project, a client asks for an extra dashboard that was not in the agreed scope, with no change to budget or deadline. What is this situation called?

options.label: Scope creep, because work is added beyond the agreed baseline
Risk transfer, because the client now takes on the added work
Progressive elaboration, because details are refined as work goes on
Crashing, because extra effort is being added to the schedule

rubric: Work added beyond the approved baseline without a change process is scope creep.
Progressive elaboration refines planned work; it does not add new deliverables.

items.prompt: A supplier has already delivered late, and the delay is now pushing back the testing phase. How should the project manager classify this?

options.label: A risk, because it could still affect the testing schedule later
An assumption, because the supplier date was taken to be true
A constraint, because the testing date limits what the project can do
An issue, because it has already happened and needs action now

rubric: A risk that has occurred becomes an issue and needs active resolution.
Calling it a risk ignores that the event has already happened.

items.prompt: Why does a one-day delay to a task on the critical path usually move the project end date?

options.label: Those tasks are the most expensive, so any delay raises the budget
Those tasks are done by senior staff, so they cannot be replaced
Those tasks have no float, so a slip passes straight to the finish
Those tasks are scheduled last, so only they decide the final date

rubric: Critical path tasks have zero float, so any delay shifts the end date.
Criticality is about float and dependencies, not cost, seniority or position.

items.prompt: On a power/interest grid, a senior executive has high power but low interest in a project. What is the usual engagement approach?

options.label: Monitor with minimal effort and no regular contact
Keep satisfied with brief, relevant updates at key points
Keep informed with frequent detailed progress newsletters
Manage closely with daily involvement in decisions

rubric: High power and low interest calls for keeping the person satisfied without overloading them.
Closely managing is for high power and high interest; informing is for low power and high interest.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a milestone in a project schedule?

options.label: A long task that groups several related activities under one heading
A zero-duration marker for a key point, like a sign-off
A buffer of extra time added to protect the final delivery date
A person who is responsible for approving each completed task

rubric: A milestone is a zero-duration marker of a significant event or achievement.
Grouped activities describe a summary task, and extra time describes a buffer.

items.prompt: Which of the following belong in a clear project scope statement? Select all that apply.

options.label: The deliverables the project will produce
Items explicitly excluded from the project
Each team member's preferred working hours
The home addresses of the vendors' staff
Acceptance criteria for the deliverables

rubric: A scope statement lists deliverables, exclusions and acceptance criteria to prevent misunderstanding.
Personal preferences and addresses are not scope definition.

items.prompt: At the midpoint of a website project, the status report shows 60% of the budget spent but only 30% of the planned work complete. The team says morale is high and nothing is blocked. What does the report most likely indicate?

options.label: Over budget for the work done; an overrun is likely
Too much contingency was set, so spending should be paused
On track, since morale is high and nothing is blocked
Ahead of schedule, because spending has been so fast

rubric: Spending twice the rate of progress means cost efficiency is poor and an overrun is likely without action.
Morale and lack of blockers do not offset the cost-to-progress gap.

items.prompt: Both paths start on day 0 and feed into Testing. Path 1: Design (3 days) then Build (5 days). Path 2: Procure (4 days) then Install (2 days). How many days of float does Path 2 have?

options.label: 8 days
0 days
2 days
6 days

rubric: Path 1 takes 8 days and Path 2 takes 6, so Path 2 has 2 days of float.
0 is the float of the critical path; 6 and 8 are path durations, not float.

items.prompt: A task has an optimistic estimate of 4 days, a most likely estimate of 6 days and a pessimistic estimate of 14 days. Using the three-point (PERT) formula (O + 4M + P) / 6, what is the expected duration?

options.label: 8 days
9 days
6 days
7 days

rubric: 8 is the simple average of the three values, and 9 is the midpoint of optimistic and pessimistic.

items.prompt: A project has a planned value of $10,000, an earned value of $8,000 and an actual cost of $9,000. What is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
rubric: SPI = EV / PV = 8,000 / 10,000 = 0.80, so the project is behind schedule.
0.89 is the cost performance index (EV / AC), and the other values invert or mix the ratios.

items.prompt: Ranking risks by exposure (probability x impact), which risk should be addressed first?

options.label: Risk A: 50% chance, $4,000 impact
Risk B: 20% chance, $15,000 impact
Risk C: 10% chance, $40,000 impact
Risk D: 80% chance, $1,000 impact

rubric: Exposures are A $2,000, B $3,000, C $4,000 and D $800, so C ranks first.
Choosing by probability alone or by the biggest-sounding number ignores the multiplication.

items.prompt: Three staff each work 40 hours a week for 4 weeks at $50 per hour. Materials cost $6,000. The sponsor requires a contingency reserve of 10% of the total. What is the budget including contingency?
rubric: Labour is $24,000, plus $6,000 materials is $30,000, and 10% contingency makes $33,000.
$32,400 applies contingency to labour only, and $30,000 omits it.

items.prompt: A stakeholder submits a new feature request after the baseline was approved. Which steps belong in a basic change control process? Select all that apply.

options.label: Start the work at once to keep the stakeholder happy
Log the request in a change register
Obtain approval before updating the baseline
Assess its impact on scope, schedule and cost
Quietly absorb the work into existing tasks

rubric: Change control logs, assesses and approves a request before the baseline changes.
Starting work early or absorbing it silently bypasses control and causes scope creep.

items.prompt: A critical-path coding task has slipped 3 days. Testing normally starts after coding finishes, but about half of the code is complete and stable. The budget has no room for extra staff, and the deadline cannot move. Which action best recovers the time?

options.label: Move the end date later without telling the sponsor yet
Hire two contractors to speed up coding, which adds cost
Drop the testing phase so the original end date is kept
Start testing the finished code while coding continues

rubric: Fast-tracking overlaps tasks that were sequential and adds no cost, fitting the constraints.
Hiring contractors is crashing and costs money; dropping testing or hiding a delay is not acceptable.

items.prompt: A project has tasks A (3 days), B (4 days), C (6 days) and D (2 days). B and C both start after A finishes, and D starts after both B and C finish. What is the minimum project duration?

options.label: 12 days, from A, the longer of B and C, and D, with D's 2 days counted twice
9 days, following the A-B-D path
11 days, following the A-C-D path
15 days, adding all four tasks in sequence

rubric: The longest path is A-C-D at 3+6+2 = 11 days.
9 days follows only the A-B-D path, and 15 days adds every task as if none ran in parallel.

items.prompt: Task X's earliest finish is the end of day 8, and its latest finish without delaying the project is the end of day 12. How much total float does Task X have?

options.label: 12 days
0 days
8 days
4 days

rubric: Total float is latest finish minus earliest finish: 12 - 8 = 4 days.
0 days confuses float with being critical, and the other values just reuse the dates.

items.prompt: A project has a budget at completion of 100,000. It was planned to be 40% complete but is actually 30% complete, having spent 35,000. What is the cost performance index (CPI), to two decimal places?
rubric: 0.75 is the schedule index, 1.17 inverts the ratio, and 0.88 compares spend with planned value.

items.prompt: A task has an optimistic estimate of 4 days, a most likely estimate of 6 days and a pessimistic estimate of 14 days. Using the three-point (PERT) weighted formula, what is the expected duration?

options.label: 6 days
8 days
9 days
7 days

rubric: 8 days is the simple average of the three values, which ignores the weighting.

items.prompt: Midway through a project, a client asks for an extra report that is not in the signed scope. Under a standard change control process, what should the project manager do first?

options.label: Ask a team lead to start the work now and record the change after delivery
Decline the request, since changes to a signed baseline need the sponsor's agreement
Add the report to the plan and absorb the effort using the existing schedule contingency
Log the request and assess its impact on scope, schedule and cost before any decision

rubric: Change control starts with logging the request and assessing its impact so an informed decision can follow.
Absorbing or pre-starting the work bypasses the process, and refusing outright ignores that baselines can change through approval.

items.prompt: A project manager is adding a newly identified supplier-delay risk to the risk register. Which entries should she complete for this risk so that it can be tracked and managed? Select all that apply.

options.label: A response action, such as placing an early order or qualifying a second supplier
An estimate of the probability the delay occurs and the impact on the schedule
The supplier's full contract payment schedule, copied in from the procurement file
A named team member who is accountable for monitoring the risk and triggering the response
The baseline cost of every work package, so the risk can be compared to the whole budget

rubric: A risk register entry records the assessment, an owner and a response.
Holiday lists and the lessons-learned report are other project documents and do not describe an individual risk.

items.prompt: A 10-week project has a team cost of 4,000 per week and fixed equipment costs of 12,000. The sponsor requires a contingency reserve of 10% of the estimated base cost. What total budget should the project manager request?
rubric: Base cost is 40,000 + 12,000 = 52,000, and 10% contingency of 5,200 gives 57,200.
56,000 applies the 10% to the team cost only, and 52,000 omits the contingency.

items.prompt: A project reports a schedule performance index (SPI) of 0.8 and a cost performance index (CPI) of 1.1. Which diagnosis do these figures best support?

options.label: The project is over budget but ahead of schedule, because spending has outpaced the work completed so far
Cost and schedule are both acceptable, because the two indices average to roughly one and offset each other
Money is used efficiently but too little work is finishing, pointing to a throughput or sequencing problem
The team is both wasting money and working slowly, so cost overrun is the main concern for the sponsor

rubric: SPI below 1 means less work is done than planned, while CPI above 1 means each dollar spent buys more than planned value.
Distractors misread the indices, treating them as averaging out or as signalling overspend.

items.prompt: A manager shortened a task by adding two people at an extra cost of 6,000. The task finished early as planned, yet the project's finish date did not move at all. Which cause best explains this?

options.label: The finish date is fixed by the budget baseline, not by the durations of tasks
The task sat on a path with float, so the longest path and finish date were unchanged
Adding people always lengthens the schedule at first, so the gains appear only later
Shortening tasks only helps when it is applied to the very last task in the schedule

rubric: Shortening a non-critical task cannot move the finish date because the critical path is unchanged.
The overhead explanation fails because the task did finish early, and the other options misstate how schedules work.

items.prompt: A project has slipped three weeks. The log shows 14 small 'quick favours' approved by individual team leads for various users, none recorded as changes. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: No enforced change control gate exists, so scope grew without any impact assessment
Users were not engaged early enough to define their requirements properly
Team leads lack the technical skills needed to say no to user requests
Estimates were too optimistic at planning, so any extra work was bound to cause delay

rubric: Many unrecorded approvals show scope growing without a gate that assesses impact, which is classic scope creep.
The other options describe possible contributors but are not supported by the evidence of unlogged approvals.

items.prompt: A PM sends a 12-page weekly report to a senior executive (high power, low interest) who never reads it. The PM holds no sessions with end users (low power, high interest), who now complain. What is the main flaw in this engagement approach?

options.label: Reports should go out less often to everyone, to reduce the overall communication workload
Engagement does not fit each group's position: executives need short updates and users need consultation
The executive should receive more detail, since high-power stakeholders must be told everything
End users should be ignored because low-power stakeholders cannot affect project success

rubric: Engagement should match power and interest: brief updates for the executive and active involvement for the interested users.
Distractors apply a blanket rule instead of tailoring communication to each group.

items.prompt: A vendor delay has a 30% chance and would cost 20,000. Mitigation costs 4,000 and cuts the chance to 10%. A penalty-clause transfer costs 3,000 and covers the full impact. Which conclusion about expected cost is correct?

options.label: Transfer and mitigation both total 6,000, so the choice depends only on preference
Transfer costs 3,000 in total, while mitigation totals 6,000, no better than doing nothing
Mitigation totals 2,000 in expected cost, so it beats transfer at 3,000
Doing nothing is cheapest at 6,000 because both responses add up-front cost

rubric: Doing nothing has an expected cost of 6,000, mitigation 4,000 + 2,000 = 6,000, and transfer 3,000.
Mitigation at 2,000 forgets the 4,000 cost of the response itself.

items.prompt: A team's tasks sit at '90% complete' for weeks and milestones keep slipping. Which are plausible root causes of this pattern? Select all that apply.

options.label: A risk register exists for the project
Progress is reported as effort spent rather than output delivered
Status meetings are held weekly
Tasks have no measurable criteria for what 'done' means
Work packages are longer than the reporting cycle

rubric: Vague done criteria, effort-based reporting and oversized work packages all hide the real progress.
Holding meetings or keeping a risk register does not explain a stuck percentage-complete figure.

items.prompt: A developer is booked for 60 hours next week: 30 on Task P, which is on the critical path, and 30 on Task Q, which has 5 days of float. Each person is capped at 40 hours a week and no one else has the skill. Which analysis is best?

options.label: Shift Task Q later within its float so the load levels out and the finish date holds
Split both tasks evenly across two weeks so each is only partly delayed beyond plan
Approve 20 hours of overtime, since any delay to either task moves the finish date
Delay Task P by a week, because the critical path can absorb a short slip in one task

rubric: Q has float, so shifting it resolves the overload without moving the finish date.
Delaying P would push the finish date, and overtime or splitting both tasks ignores the available float.

items.prompt: At month 6 a project reports PV 200k, EV 170k and AC 150k. A new PM says: 'SPI is 0.85, so the critical path is 15% late.' Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: The project is ahead on cost, and that favourable variance offsets the schedule variance, so the net position is neutral and no recovery action is needed.
CPI of 1.13 means the team is efficient, so SPI will recover automatically because the same efficiency applies to the remaining work.
SPI of 0.85 shows the critical path is 15% late, because earned value is measured against the baseline activities that drive the end date.
Cost is fine, but SPI 0.85 only shows less work earned than planned; it does not show if critical-path work slipped.

rubric: SPI aggregates all work and says nothing about which activities slipped, so critical-path impact needs schedule analysis.
Distractors treat EV metrics as path-specific or let cost performance offset schedule variance.

items.prompt: Two parallel paths feed the final milestone. Path A is 40 days and critical; Path B is 38 days. One task on Path B slips by 3 days, with all else equal. By how many days does the project finish date move?

options.label: 1 day
2 days
3 days
0 days

rubric: Path B becomes 41 days, 1 day longer than Path A, so the finish moves by 1 day.
Choosing 0 ignores that the slip exceeds float; choosing 3 ignores the 2 days of float.

items.prompt: Developers keep doing small extras requested directly by client staff in daily chats. No request exceeds an hour, yet the project is 12% over budget against an unchanged scope baseline. What is the root cause?

options.label: Client staff are acting in bad faith, so the contract should be tightened until they stop making further requests.
Estimates carried too little padding, so any small extra request pushes the budget over its baseline.
Requests bypass the change control path, so their cumulative effort is never assessed, approved or added to the baseline.
Small requests are too minor to count as scope, so the baseline must be defined at finer granularity to catch them.

rubric: The failure is the missing change-control gate, which lets many small unassessed changes accumulate.
Distractors blame estimates, client motives or baseline granularity rather than process.

items.prompt: A risk register lists three separate medium risks, each 20% likely: supplier delivery delay, supplier quality defects and supplier staff turnover. What is the main flaw in treating them as three independent entries?

options.label: They share one root cause in a single supplier, so they are likely correlated and the combined exposure is higher than it looks.
Medium risks add little value to a register, since a named owner and response plan are normally justified only for high-scoring risks.
Three risks tied to one supplier look like double counting, so they should usually be merged into one entry scored at the highest of the three.
Their likelihoods should be added to give a 60% chance of one event, which is the usual way to score related risks for the same supplier.

rubric: Common-cause risks are correlated, so scoring them independently understates aggregate exposure.
Distractors invent summing rules, drop medium risks or wrongly merge them.

items.prompt: Every team member is allocated 100% across two projects, yet tasks wait days for handoffs and lead time is double the effort estimates. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Handoffs are slow because members dislike the other project, so morale should be addressed before capacity is looked at.
Effort estimates are inaccurate, so every task should be re-estimated before any change to allocation or workload is considered.
Allocation is correct and delays come only from task dependencies, which can be fixed only by adding more staff to each task.
Fully loaded people have no slack, so work queues behind other work and switching between projects adds hidden overhead.

rubric: Full utilisation leaves no buffer, creating queues and context-switch cost that inflate lead time.
Distractors blame estimates, morale or dependencies instead of the loading itself.

items.prompt: A project reported green for ten weeks, then turned red with six weeks of slippage. Which reporting practices could plausibly explain the late surprise? Select all that apply.

options.label: Risks are reviewed at every steering meeting with named owners.
Milestones are tracked weekly against a baselined plan with exit criteria.
Progress is judged on tasks started rather than on remaining effort to finish.
Task owners self-report percent complete with no objective done criteria.
Bad news is escalated only after the team has tried to recover quietly.

rubric: Subjective percent complete, start-based progress and delayed escalation all hide slippage until it is large.
Baselined milestones with exit criteria and regular risk reviews expose problems early.

items.prompt: A PM crashes the critical activity 'integration' by 5 days by adding contractors, expecting the finish date to move 5 days earlier. The schedule moves only 2 days earlier, and the contractor cost was as planned. Which explanation best fits?

options.label: A parallel path only 2 days shorter than the old critical path became critical, so it now limits the finish date.
Contractor onboarding always cancels exactly 60% of crashing gains, so only 2 days of 5 can be realised.
Fast-tracking was used instead of crashing, and fast-tracking returns only 40% of the planned reduction.
Crashing shortens only cost, not duration, so the remaining gain will appear after the project closes.

rubric: Shortening the critical path shifts criticality to a near-critical path, capping the gain at that path's float.
Distractors invent fixed loss ratios or confuse crashing with fast-tracking.

items.prompt: At initiation a sponsor needs a funding figure for a project using novel technology with unclear requirements. Criteria: honest about uncertainty, usable for approval, low effort now. Which estimating approach is best?

options.label: A ranged analogy-based estimate using three-point values, stated assumptions and refinement at each stage gate.
One detailed bottom-up estimate by task, since a precise number builds sponsor confidence in the funding request.
The previous project's actual cost unchanged, since a historical figure avoids any bias from optimism in the team.
A fixed figure with 50% padding added to every task, so no range ever needs to be presented to the sponsor.

rubric: A range with assumptions and refinement is honest, quick and supports staged approval.
Distractors give false precision, ignore differences between projects or hide uncertainty in padding.

items.prompt: A key vendor may fail: 20% likelihood, 200k impact, and no other impacts matter. Judge by total expected cost. Which response is best?

options.label: Accept the risk: expected loss of 40k, with no upfront spend required.
Buy cover for 12k that reimburses the full impact: total expected cost is 12k.
Qualify a second vendor for 25k: the risk is removed, so total cost is 25k.
Mitigate for 30k: expected loss falls to 10k, so total expected cost is 40k.

rubric: Cover costs 12k with no residual loss, the lowest total expected cost of the four.
Mitigation breaks even with accepting; the second vendor costs more than cover.

items.prompt: A project has a regulatory deadline in 5 months. Compliance reports have fixed specifications, while the user interface will likely change. Criteria: meet the deadline, absorb UI change, keep compliance traceable. Which approach is best?

options.label: A fully predictive plan for all work, so every change is blocked until after the deadline has passed.
A hybrid: fixed-scope plan for compliance reports and iterative delivery for the UI within a time-boxed backlog.
A fully agile approach with no upfront scope, so the deadline is met by dropping whatever is unfinished.
Two separate projects with separate sponsors and plans, so each approach never needs to coordinate with the other.

rubric: The hybrid matches each work type to its stability and protects the fixed deadline.
Distractors apply one method to everything or split the work so coordination fails.

items.prompt: Contingency is zero and go-live date is fixed. Criteria: protect date and budget, satisfy legal obligations. Requests: (1) regulator-mandated field, 3 days; (2) sponsor dashboard, 5 days, 'just fit it in'; (3) label rename, 1 day, no benefit. Which decision is best?

options.label: Approve the dashboard first, because the sponsor's request usually outranks regulatory items when priorities conflict.
Reject all three requests, because with zero contingency a change cannot be accepted, even one required by law.
Approve all three requests and ask the team to absorb the 9 days through overtime, keeping date and budget.
Approve the regulator field and defer the dashboard and label rename, keeping date and budget unchanged.

rubric: The mandatory item is met by swapping out lower-value scope, keeping constraints intact.
Distractors absorb work silently, refuse legal changes or rank sponsor wishes above compliance.

items.prompt: A steering committee decides monthly whether to continue, descope or stop a project. Criteria: supports that decision, short, hard to game. Which report format is best?

options.label: A red/amber/green dashboard per workstream, set by each lead's own judgement of how their workstream is doing.
A full 400-line task-level Gantt chart, so committee members can locate any issue themselves whenever they need to.
A narrative of team achievements this month, written by the PM to show momentum and motivate every stakeholder.
One page: forecast cost and finish versus baseline, top risks with exposure, decisions needed and milestone evidence.

rubric: Forecast variance, exposure and evidence directly support a continue/descope/stop decision and resist spin.
Distractors bury the decision in detail, rely on subjective ratings or emphasise morale.

items.prompt: A sponsor demands a 20% budget cut with the date unchanged. Criteria: keep the date, protect quality, keep the sponsor informed of trade-offs. Which responses are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Remove the contingency reserve without telling anyone, to meet the new figure.
Accept the cut with full scope, assuming productivity will rise to compensate.
Cut testing effort by 20% because testing is not visible in the deliverable.
Re-baseline cost through change control, recording descoped items and added risks.
Present scope options ranked by value so the sponsor chooses what is cut.

rubric: Value-ranked options and a documented re-baseline meet all three criteria.
Distractors sacrifice quality, rely on hope or hide the loss of contingency.

items.prompt: A project is 8 weeks late against a 20-week baseline after a vendor failure outside the team's control. The PM proposes rewriting the baseline so status shows green. The sponsor wants a credible view of performance. Which course is best?

options.label: Split the remaining work into a new project with a fresh baseline, so the original delay vanishes from all reporting.
Rebaseline through formal change control approved by the sponsor, keeping the original baseline and variance history on record.
Keep the original baseline and report red until the end, since any rebaseline would hide the true cause of the delay.
Overwrite the baseline quietly, since the delay was outside the team's control and so should not count against them.

rubric: Formal rebaselining gives a realistic forward plan while preserving transparency about the earlier variance.
Distractors hide the variance or leave reporting permanently uninformative.

items.prompt: A team pads every task estimate by about 50% yet routinely finishes projects late. Judge which diagnosis best fits this pattern.

options.label: Padding is still too small; doubling every task estimate removes lateness because each task will then finish early
Task-level padding is consumed by student syndrome and Parkinson's law, so a pooled buffer at the path end protects the date better
Padding works, so the cause is weak tracking; weekly status reports alone would turn the padded time into early finishes
Lateness comes from having too many tasks; merging them into a few large work packages removes the need for any buffer

rubric: Safety hidden in individual tasks is typically wasted through late starts and filling available time, so pooled buffers are more efficient.
Distractors assume more padding or reporting fixes behaviour that padding itself causes.

items.prompt: A project with a budget at completion (BAC) of 400k is at its 50% time mark: PV 200k, EV 160k, AC 200k. The 40k cost overrun came from a one-off penalty that will not recur, and all remaining work will cost exactly as budgeted. Which estimate at completion (EAC) is most defensible?
rubric: When the variance is atypical, EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 200 + 240 = 440k.
500k applies BAC/CPI, which wrongly assumes the overrun trend continues.

items.prompt: You may start mitigation on only one risk this month. Criteria: act first where waiting removes the mitigation option, regardless of raw exposure. Which risk do you pick?

options.label: A likely supplier delay costing about 60k, where the long-lead order must be placed within two weeks or the option lapses
A near-certain minor scope creep costing 5k, which the existing change control process already handles each week
A regulator rule change worth 900k, expected in 18 months, where mitigation can start at any time before then
A moderate-chance key-person loss costing 200k, where a low-cost cross-training fix remains available at any time

rubric: The stated criterion is a closing mitigation window, which only the supplier risk has.
Distractors tempt you to rank by size of exposure, though those options stay open.

items.prompt: Standard stakeholder advice says to only 'keep satisfied' high-power, low-interest people. Judge where this advice breaks down most seriously.

options.label: When the executive attends many meetings, because frequent attendance proves the person has interest and needs full engagement
When the executive dislikes email, because the communication channel then matters more than the content of any update
When the executive has a long title, because seniority alone means the person should be treated as a core team member
When the executive controls a phase-2 funding gate, because a surprise at that gate can halt the project despite low interest

rubric: Latent veto power at a later gate means low interest still needs early, tailored briefings.
Distractors rely on surface cues like title or habits rather than decision influence.

items.prompt: Criteria: the PM is accountable for identified risks, the sponsor owns the approved baseline. Which reserve governance best fits?

options.label: Both reserves are released by the PM once a task slips, since schedule delay is itself the trigger that justifies drawing on any reserve
The sponsor approves each draw on both reserves, since contingency is part of the approved budget and any use of it changes the baseline
The PM controls both reserves, since accountability for delivery requires discretion over unallocated funds when unplanned work appears
The PM draws contingency for identified risks; management reserve for unplanned work needs sponsor approval and a baseline change

rubric: Contingency covers known risks under PM authority; management reserve covers unknowns and alters the baseline, so the sponsor approves.
Distractors collapse the two reserves or remove the accountability split.

items.prompt: A client needs a capped budget, but requirements will emerge as work proceeds. Which commercial approaches fit these criteria? Select all that apply.

options.label: Phased delivery with a discovery phase, then a fixed price for each later phase once scope is clearer
Fixed price on the full specification written today, with no provision for revisiting scope as learning emerges
Cost-plus with no cap, so the supplier can respond to every new requirement without limit on spend
Time-and-materials with a not-to-exceed cap and a prioritised backlog that is cut to fit the cap

rubric: A capped T&M and phased fixed prices both bound spend while allowing scope to emerge.
Full upfront fixed price ignores uncertainty; uncapped cost-plus breaks the cap.

items.prompt: A project is three weeks behind. The launch date is fixed by regulation, only the 8% contingency may be spent, and quality failures are unacceptable. Critical-path tasks include mandatory compliance work, optional features and splittable testing. Which recovery option is best?

options.label: Add people to every critical task, including the compliance work, since extra staff shorten each task's duration in direct proportion to headcount
Request a launch extension, since a regulatory date is a preference that sponsors routinely agree to move when the team is behind
Defer optional features and crash the splittable testing within contingency, as both shorten the path without adding rework risk
Overlap all dependent critical tasks, since fast-tracking costs nothing extra and the rework it causes is unlikely to threaten the date

rubric: Descoping and crashing splittable work meets the date, budget and quality criteria.
Fast-tracking adds rework risk; adding staff to non-splittable work gives diminishing returns.

items.prompt: Design a change control process meeting these constraints: small changes decided within a day, large changes decided at sponsor level, and a full audit trail. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Every change goes to the sponsor for a signature, since a single approval route keeps the audit trail simple
Tiered thresholds: the PM decides small changes, the sponsor decides large ones, and all are logged
A change board meets monthly to decide every request, since regular scheduling keeps the audit trail consistent
The team makes all changes informally and the PM documents them at project close, since that keeps delivery fast

rubric: Tiering gives speed for small changes and escalation for large ones, with logging as the audit trail.
Other options fail the one-day constraint or the audit constraint.

items.prompt: One engineer is needed for tasks B and C, which are parallel (4 days each). C is critical; B has 5 days of float. No new hires are allowed. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: Do C first, then B, since B's finish then stays inside its float and the critical path is unchanged
Alternate B and C daily, since splitting time evenly lets both finish at similar times
Hire a contractor for B, since removing the resource conflict is the quickest way to protect the date
Do B first, then C, since starting with the task that has more float keeps the engineer's workload steady

rubric: C first, then B finishes on day 8, within B's float, with no delay and no cost.
B first delays critical C; alternating adds switching loss; hiring breaks the constraint.

items.prompt: A 12-month program has requirements firm for only 3 months and a fixed annual budget. Which planning design meets both constraints?

options.label: Detail the next 3 months, hold phase milestones and budget envelopes beyond, and replan at a quarterly gate
Set a 12-month plan with 40% padding on most tasks, so the padding absorbs requirement changes and replanning is rarely needed
Plan all 12 months in task-level detail now, so a single complete baseline gives the most reliable cost and schedule control
Plan only to month 3 in detail and fund later months as requirements firm up, since long-range plans tend to be wrong

rubric: Rolling-wave planning fits partial knowledge while staying inside the fixed budget through envelopes and gates.
Full detail is false precision; no planning loses budget control; padding is wasteful.

items.prompt: A risk register says only: 'If the vendor fails, switch to the backup vendor.' What addition most makes this response executable?

options.label: Re-score the risk's probability and impact each month so the team sees when exposure has grown beyond tolerance
A measurable trigger date, a named owner and pre-approved funding drawn from contingency
A lessons-learned entry scheduled at project close so the vendor outcome is documented for later projects
A secondary risk entry for the backup vendor with its own probability, impact and qualitative rating

rubric: A response needs a trigger, an owner and authorised funds to be actionable.
Other options improve monitoring or records but don't make the response executable.

items.prompt: Design a 15-minute steering committee report that supports decisions and stays honest about delivery. Which design fits?

options.label: A 40-slide deck of all task statuses, since full detail avoids any suggestion of hiding bad news
A verbal update only, since discussion is faster and lets the sponsor probe whatever matters to them
One page with a green status for each workstream, since colour ratings are fastest to read at a glance
One page showing baseline versus forecast date and cost, trends, and top risks with the decisions needed

rubric: Baseline-versus-forecast with decisions fits time limits and keeps the report honest.
The other options bury the message, hide detail in colours, or leave no record.

items.prompt: A charter draft for a cross-department project has vague goals and no sign-off rules. Which additions best make it a usable foundation? Select all that apply.

options.label: A full task-level Gantt chart covering every activity to close
A calendar of team social events through the project
An explicit out-of-scope list that stakeholders have reviewed
Measurable success criteria agreed with the sponsor
A named authority for scope, time and cost trade-off decisions

rubric: Success criteria, exclusions and decision authority fix the gaps of vague goals and no sign-off rules.
A detailed Gantt is premature for a charter; the social calendar is irrelevant.

items.prompt: A project is 40% complete, the sponsor has lost confidence, and three stakeholders make conflicting demands. The original baseline is no longer achievable. Which recovery plan best restores credibility while preserving accountability?

options.label: Build an independent estimate to complete, agree a prioritised minimum scope with the sponsor, and report against a new baseline while keeping the old one
Freeze stakeholder change requests and hold the original scope, reporting only the current-period variance until the sponsor sees recovery trend upward again
Keep the original baseline and add overtime and extra staff to the critical path, since re-baselining would signal weakness and reset accountability to zero
Replace the PM and let the new lead re-plan from scratch, discarding the old baseline so earlier variances do not distort the new reporting

rubric: Re-baselining on a credible estimate with agreed priorities restores trust while the preserved old baseline keeps accountability.
Other options hide the problem or leave the unachievable plan in place.
